But listen:
The room can sound muffled and even seem a little claustrophobic without the windows open. Windows are not just about light and views but also about letting in air and, by implication, the rest of the world. They are transparent membranes and portals.
A room sounds very different when a window is open. Sound defines, animates and enlarges the architecture.
If only subliminally, we also know, by contrast, when sound spoils architecture because it fails to correspond to function. The bygone Shea Stadium in Queens was joyless partly because the design of its low, wide semicircle dissipated the sound of a cheering crowd into Flushing Bay. Fenway Park in Boston is the reverse; it concentrates hometown joy.
Sound and form go together. We presume it’s a truism that a large, airy space provides us with more aural room than a small one. But imagine yourself having a private conversation in a crowded elevator where a half-dozen other people are talking as well. Now picture yourself having that same conversation with only a single other person in the elevator.
In which case would you be more comfortable saying what’s on your mind? There can be privacy in a crowd.
A few years ago I accompanied Peter Zumthor, the Swiss architect, to a tiny chapel he designed in Sumvitg, Switzerland, a mountain village. The chapel is a shingled, one-room building, shaped a little like a ship. The latch on the door made a loud clunk when it caught the strike. My footsteps creaked on the soft floorboards. Mr. Zumthor had masterminded the effects, orchestrating materials, space and acoustics into a satisfying whole.
“Sound is really important,” Ricardo Scofidio, from Diller Scofidio & Renfro, who helped design the High Line, acknowledged. But then he said, unless you’re an architect designing a concert hall, “you’re not thinking about how you might produce a specific sound.” He added, “That’s partly because the process of making models and drawings doesn’t allow for it.” Besides, clients don’t ask much about what a house will sound like.
And yet.
Mr. Scofidio called me back. He said that since we had spoken, he had found himself conjuring the sounds of certain places. He recalled the acoustics of a round elevator in the Cooper Union building in New York, as well as Grand Central Terminal, “where suddenly you’re aware of your footsteps, and that sound lets you feel your physical presence in the space.”
Ambient noise in Grand Central rises upward and outward, toward the hall’s immense ceiling, embodying the impression of the terminal as a soaring gateway to a great metropolis, promising adventure.
By contrast, Penn Station’s low ceilings suppress sound, which becomes hard to make out, an audible metaphor for its rat’s maze of architecture.
“You feel that your life is being lost in a room where sound dies,” pointed out the architect Renzo Piano. “We need reverberation.”
The other day I returned to the New York Public Library at Fifth Avenue and 42nd Street, just to listen. Sound provided room to think. The beauty of the high ceilings and big windows was amplified, and humanized, by the scratching of chairs and the clomp-clomp of boots on hardwood floors. Readers pored over books, texted and daydreamed.
Even a place of shared silence is never really silent.

Dear Diary:
Last winter my wife and I were on our way to a friend’s apartment to watch TV when we came across an elderly man sprawled on his back in the crosswalk. He was lying on the frozen street at 72nd and Broadway with his bags scattered in the snow and a dazed M.T.A. driver standing next to his bus. We waited at the light. Didn’t hear any sirens, and the other bystanders were just standing by.
Neither my wife nor I are trained first responders by any means. She knows CPR and I grew up hunting and took some first-aid courses, because being gored or accidentally shot in the woods was not going to be my way out. Coupled with the fact we originally came from the land of unpredictable sneaky earthquakes, I made it a habit to carry a flashlight and mini trauma kit in my bag.
I slapped on the nitrile gloves and did an injury assessment while keeping the man calm and talking. No bones poking out or bleeding lacerations. Only thing we could do was keep his neck immobilized and mind conscious. He was surprisingly pleasant, given his circumstances. Eyes still closed, he whispered to me, “It’s a nice night, isn’t it?”
We’re losing him! He continued, “I knew I could count on another New Yorker to help.” Yup, definite head injury. His mouth widened into a smile and we kept idle chatter.
An officer came a few minutes later. My wife and I got up without saying anything to the cop or the recumbent man and continued on our way to watch “The Bachelor.”

The adage that “you can’t teach an old dog new tricks” certainly does not apply to criminal laws, which are routinely used in new situations hardly conceived when they were adopted. That will play out this week in New York when a judge will have to decide whether daily fantasy sports constitute gambling under laws adopted long before these contests were even possible.
New York State’s attorney general,
Eric T. Schneiderman
,
filed lawsuits
against the two leading daily fantasy sports companies, FanDuel and DraftKings, asking for an injunction to stop them from operating, saying that they are violating the prohibition on gambling that is part of
the state’s constitution
.
Like many such legal disputes, this one centers on a seemingly simple phrase in the definition of gambling in
New York State’s penal law
: “A person engages in gambling when he stakes or risks something of value upon the outcome of a contest of chance or a future contingent event not under his control or influence.” Chance means that “the outcome depends in a material degree upon an element of chance, notwithstanding that skill of the contestants may also be a factor therein.”
In
a memorandum filed
as part of the case, Mr. Schneiderman asserts that daily fantasy sports “is nothing more than a rebranding of sports betting” which is “plainly illegal.” He stepped up the criticism in an editorial in The
New York Daily News
when he called the argument that the contests did not qualify as gambling because they involved a measure of skill “nonsense.”
Showing how important the issue has become, DraftKings brought in
David Boies
, one of the country’s leading litigators, to fight the attorney general’s case. FanDuel has temporarily suspended operations in New York, while DraftKings continues to allow residents there to play. A hearing is set for Wednesday in the New York Supreme Court in Manhattan to consider Mr. Schneiderman’s request.
In a conference call on Friday, Mr. Boies challenged the claim that daily fantasy sports contests clearly violate the law, asserting that they have been legal for the past eight years the company has operated.

Like most gamblers, winners claim their victories were the result of skill, while losers blame bad luck — a quarterback’s ill-timed interception or an untimely injury to a key player are the usual culprits — so there is certainly an element of both in daily fantasy sports. Figuring out what is a “future contingent event” outside the player’s control or influence is also far from clear because the contest’s outcome can be attributed to the games played on the field as much as the decision to select certain players to compose a fantasy team.
Mr. Schneiderman’s complaint emphasizes the promotional advertising by FanDuel and DraftKings to show it is a form of gambling, pointing to the get-quick-rich claims that make it sound more like winning the lottery than a test of skill and knowledge. But advertisements are rarely evidence of what happens in the real world because not everything can be the best, brightest or biggest, as often promised to consumers.

On the flip side, claims that the government is changing the rules after allowing the companies to operate for years is not how the law is usually interpreted. Just because everyone else drives fast does not change the speed limit, regardless of whether it is routinely unenforced. So Mr. Schneiderman’s decision to try to put a stop to contests his office considers a violation of the gambling prohibition is not affected by whether he arrived a bit late to the game.
It should not come as any great surprise that a law adopted long before the advent of daily fantasy sports is not as unambiguous as the opposing sides have proclaimed it to be. So any decision in the trial court is likely to be appealed by the losing side, which means any final resolution of the scope of the gambling prohibition is probably months away.
The larger question is whether shutting down daily fantasy sports is the best way to address issues raised about how they involve elements of gambling. The contests can be feed the addiction of compulsive gamblers, as
a front-page article in The New York Times
on Monday describes how easily the unregulated world of fantasy sports can be abused.
The world survived the elimination of most online poker sites from the United States a few years ago, so cracking down on this newest form of entertainment may not have too much of an impact. The contests are popular with casual players who do not abuse them, however, so denying access to what is for many a harmless form of entertainment may be overkill.
Massachusetts has gone in a different direction that may signal a better way to deal with issues related to daily fantasy sports contests. The state attorney general, Maura Healey,
proposed regulations
that would curtail how the companies operate to address potential problems related to gambling and maintaining the integrity of the contests.
The new rules would prohibit minors from playing the games and require companies to take steps to limit abusive practices by gamblers, such as setting deposit limits and not marketing to those who identify themselves as having gambling problems. Contests based on college or high school athletes would be prohibited, and companies could not advertise or promote themselves at amateur or school venues.
More drastic measures could affect how profitable the daily fantasy sports companies could be if the regulations were adopted broadly. The proposal would limit players to one account per company and require “reasonable measures” to verify their identity to limit anyone from playing through multiple accounts, including efforts to block proxy servers that might hide who is actually entering contests. Nor could a company extend credit to a player, further distinguishing this type of play from Las Vegas-style gambling. The rules would also limit deposits to $1,000 per month unless the company verifies a player’s ability to sustain higher losses, another step to keep participants from risking too much.
An issue that has come up with the daily fantasy sports contests is the fact that the top players win the bulk of the prizes, including many who are employees of other companies running contests. Ms. Healey’s proposal would prohibit employees and those with access to inside information about how teams are being put together from participating, along with professional athletes and their agents.

the top spot

a rush of development

MONTAUK, N.Y. —  With the ocean roaring in front of them, guests relaxed under white umbrellas on a recent summer afternoon here. Stacked against a hill behind them were the villas and cottages of the Panoramic View, the beneficiary of one of the
most audacious frauds in Long Island history
.
And, it turns out, one heck of an investment.
In a Ponzi-meets-“The Producers” fraud, two brothers-in-law tricked investors out of $96 million, diverting much of the money, which investors thought was going into managed funds, to prop up the then-faltering Panoramic View.
But in a remarkable twist, the men who lost so much of others’ money turned out to have a way with real estate. The Panoramic View was such a good investment that now, two years after the men were arrested, the investors stand a chance of recouping some of their money — a rarity in fraud cases.
That prospect has the federal government in charge of selling a luscious piece of Hamptons real estate. And the government, the victims, the defendants and a federal judge are in unusual agreement: sell high.
Brian R. Callahan, one of the brothers-in-law, who positioned himself as a hedge-fund manager, had a simple pitch: Invest with me, and I will invest in a group of other hedge funds. He raised $90 million from about 45 investors and promised them he would route the money to funds that were as close to household names as the hedge-fund world gets, like SAC Capital Advisors, Paulson Advantage Plus and one of Carl C. Icahn’s funds.
The money would be liquid, and they could withdraw with a couple of days’ notice, he told investors.
“They were sold as very safe investments,” said a Texas investor, who was introduced to Mr. Callahan through a friend and invested several hundred thousand with him in 2011; she spoke on the condition that she not to be named because her family did not know she had lost her retirement money. “That’s all I really wanted. New York should be grateful that the Yale Center for British Art in New Haven is closed for renovations. As a result, eight canvases by the inimitable English painter George Stubbs, one of the great artists of the 18th century, have been lent to the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Works by Stubbs are scarce in this town: The Met has one painting, and there’s a drawing at the Frick Collection. This makes “
Paintings by George Stubbs From the Yale Center for British Art
” a rare and thrilling treat.
Born in 1724, Stubbs was celebrated during the 1760s and ’70s foremost for his elegantly precise, exquisitely composed paintings of thoroughbreds: the racehorses and the hunters often found on English country estates. He also painted dogs and wild animals, as well as hunting, shooting and farming scenes and several harrowing images of a wild horse being attacked by a lion, presaging the feverish Romanticism of Henry Fuseli, Théodore Géricault and Eugène Delacroix.
But Stubbs usually tends toward a restrained neo-Classicism, with a democratic undercurrent. He seems to have been drawn more to horses and the people who tended and raced them than to society patrons — whom, after all, he generally portrayed only in the company of their mounts. And Stubbs’s ultimate subject may be the open English countryside and by implication, the largeness of the world. It is telling, at least in the paintings at the Met, that his figures are deliberately small relative to the scenes they inhabit.
Despite his considerable success, Stubbs was already out of style by the time he died in 1806, after which he was consigned to the lower regions of art history as a horse painter, a label that stuck for nearly two centuries. One factor in this revival was the collector Paul Mellon, who bought his first Stubbs painting in 1936 and went on to acquire many more. The Yale Center, which opened in 1977 with a large gift from Mr. Mellon’s collection, ultimately received 29 of his Stubbses.
Stubbs’s first museum exhibition was not until 1951, and a 1984 show at the Tate finally secured his stature. Today, his best paintings — mostly those of horses — have an enduring “shock of the new,” akin to that of certain works by Goya, Degas, J. M. W. Turner and Winslow Homer. In particular, the strikingly low, plain, implicitly modern horizon line that Stubbs gave his racehorse portraits in the early 1760s recurs in Goya’s portrait of the Duchess of Alba in mourning, from the 1790s.

Stubbs was born in Liverpool, where his father was a successful currier, or leather craftsman, whose constant handling of animal hides may have spurred his son’s childhood interest in anatomy. Although Stubbs studied briefly with the landscape painter Hamlet Winstanley, he was largely self-taught. This included a long stint studying human anatomy at York County Hospital, during which he illustrated a book on midwifery and taught himself engraving in the process.
His growing interest in horses then led to a truly arduous bout of autodidacticism. As is oft recounted, in 1756, Stubbs rented a remote farmhouse in York and worked in a kind of single-minded frenzy for 18 months with Mary Spencer (who later became his wife). He hung horse cadavers on hooks, arranged them in naturalistic poses and alternately dissected and drew for about six weeks — at which point a fresh cadaver would be needed.

Settling in London in 1759, Stubbs sought patronage for an illustrated book on horses. Interest was not forthcoming, but his drawings attracted abundant commissions to paint the horses of landed gentry. The book, “The Anatomy of the Horse,” was published in 1766, and only after Stubbs himself engraved its 18 plates, in addition to writing its substantial text. The work’s groundbreaking accuracy echoes throughout Stubbs’s art and that of his imitators.
The greatest Stubbs in this show is the quietly magnificent “
Turf, With Jockey Up, at Newmarket
,” from about 1765, in which a racehorse, Turf, with his jockey on board, and an austere rubbing-down house are seen against a vast sky at a course in Suffolk. Carefully linked by the overlap of the steed’s bobbed tail and the house, the geometric structure and the muscular horse hint at an equestrian monument for the common man, albeit with the hero placed next to, rather than atop, his pedestal. But the sky and surrounding space are larger still, as indicated by the distant trees visible around the horse’s legs. A white post at the right edge of the painting suggests the track just beyond; man and horse are about to race, and thus the mood of concentration, whose fulcrum is the lean face of the jockey, a portrait worthy of Goya.
A pendant to this work is nearby, the small “
Newmarket Heath With a Rubbing-Down House
,” also from about 1765, which has the same nearly fish-eye vista, without Turf and the jockey. It is one of only two horseless landscapes Stubbs painted, both of Newmarket.
The remaining pictures include four sequential shooting scenes that follow two of Stubbs’s friends out for a day of tracking small game with their two dogs. At ease in nature, the hunters start out from a farm painted in the style of Dutch landscapists like Jacob van Ruisdael and Meindert Hobbema. Next, they are shown loading their guns. In the third, most cinematic painting, the dogs flush a quail, and one of the men shoots it out of the sky. Finally, we see the hunters in a forest, resting and assembling a small pile of birds and hare, in a cathedral-like space.
The eighth painting, “
Freeman, the Earl of Clarendon’s Gamekeeper, With a Dying Doe and Hound
,” from 1800, is a relatively upscale hunting scene, the conclusion of a chase. Stubbs’s powers have declined, but it is nonetheless a poignant scene. Freeman has pulled off the dog and is about to cut the doe’s throat. The dog looks yearningly toward Freeman, who looks implacably toward us, his visibly matted hair showing signs of effort. A black silk top hat, a sign of his rank, glimmers on the ground behind him, his gun carefully placed across it to avoid the damp. We see a man doing his job flawlessly and respectfully, like the jockeys and the grooms.
The Stubbs works share a large permanent-collection gallery at the Met (No. 629, to be exact), and this makes for a fine comparison with over 20 paintings by other English artists or artists working in England during Stubbs’s lifetime. Nearly half are big, glamorous portraits, in the grand style, by Joshua Reynolds, a founder of the Royal Academy of Arts — where Stubbs and other painters of animals had only limited memberships — as well as by Thomas Gainsborough, Thomas Lawrence and George Romney. The subjects in these works are larger than life, with swaths of lavish silks and gorgeous brushwork. They take up a great deal of canvas, and nature is usually relegated to the margins. Beside these peacocks, the Stubbs canvases can start to look like little wrens. But not quite.
Stubbs treated all living creatures equally, regardless of class or species. His impeccable, carefully ordered realism was less a style than a deep understanding of our place in the workings of the world.

LOS ANGELES —  Hollywood is prone to superlatives, but this one is truly jaw dropping:
“American Sniper,”
which arrived in wide release on Friday, is expected to sell about $105.2 million in tickets in North America over the four-day holiday weekend.
While America’s coastal intelligentsia busied itself with chatter over little-seen art dramas like “Boyhood” and “Birdman,” everyday Americans showed up en masse for a patriotic, pro-family picture that played more like a summer superhero blockbuster than an R-rated war drama with six Oscar nominations.
Directed by Clint Eastwood
and starring
Bradley Cooper
, “American Sniper” joins another unexpected hit, Angelina Jolie’s
“Unbroken,”
in turning out a conservative, heartland crowd that surprised Hollywood in its size. “Tennessee, Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico — all absolutely massive,” said Dan Fellman, president of domestic distribution at Warner Bros., which released “American Sniper.”
But unlike “Unbroken,” Mr. Eastwood’s film has also been
nominated
for best picture at the Oscars. Until now, the best picture race, with small films like “Birdman” and “Boyhood” in the running, has been sorely missing a breakout hit — considered a crucial factor for the ratings success of the ceremony, which will be broadcast live on Feb. 22.
“American Sniper,” which received reviews that were strong but not euphoric, was adapted from a best-selling autobiography of the same name by Chris Kyle, a member of the Navy SEALs who was credited with enough confirmed kills in Iraq and Afghanistan to rank as the most deadly sniper in American history. Mr. Kyle was killed in 2013 at a Texas gun range by an emotionally troubled veteran he was trying to help.
“The previews looked really intense, and I was curious about it being a true story,” said Eric Davidson, 19, who saw the movie with two friends in Indianapolis on Friday. “I immediately recommended it on Twitter. Everyone’s talking about it.”
The film gave Hollywood its biggest January weekend opening ever, beating “Avatar,” which took in $74.4 million in 2010, after adjusting for inflation. Mr. Eastwood’s film ranks as the largest R-rated release in history for Imax, where the film took in $11.5 million, beating the previous record-holder, “Prometheus.” Making “American Sniper” look even better: “Blackhat,” a cyberthriller from the director Michael Mann, bombed in its first weekend. “Blackhat,” which cost Legendary Entertainment an estimated $70 million to make and was released by Universal Pictures, is expected to take in $4.6 million over the four-day weekend, according to Rentrak, which compiles box office data.
Warner, which produced “American Sniper” with Village Roadshow for $58 million, initially planned to release the film next Christmas. Mr. Eastwood, 84, typically makes one film a year and his 2014 entry was “Jersey Boys,” which fizzled in July, taking in a total of $47 million.

On a brisk night in Milan last month, the chic concept store
10 Corso Como
was packed with Italian fashion journalists and socialites young and old.
Sita Abellán, a blue-haired model and D.J. stylishly dressed head to toe in Moschino, was spinning house music. Attractive servers dressed in white shirts and black trousers passed out glasses of prosecco. And at 6:30, the fashion designer Jeremy Scott arrived with Martin Pos, the founder of Cybex.
Is
Cybex
a cutting-edge fashion label? Far from it. The company, based in southern Germany, makes highly engineered baby strollers and car seats that have become popular among jet-setting European and Hollywood parents.
In 2013, Cybex commissioned Mr. Scott, the creative director of Moschino, to design a fashion-forward line of diaper bags, car seats and strollers. He obliged, using a wildly patterned fabric with cartoonish images of fast food. This time, Mr. Scott created
a more minimalist line
: all-black baby carriers, car seats and sturdy three-in-one strollers with large gold wings on either side.
The items, which are sold exclusively through 10 Corso Como until the end of the year and will be available at additional stores in 2016, range from $129.95 for the baby carrier to $1,799.95 for a three-in-one travel system.
“My first designs for Cybex were very colorful and playful,” Mr. Scott said. “This time I decided to go in the opposite direction: all black with gold details. A little bit ‘pimp my stroller.’”
Mr. Scott, 40, does not have children, so he asked friends who are parents to try out the products. “Like Fergie and Gwen Stefani,” he said. “Also an old friend of mine who I went to school with.”
Even without their input, Mr. Scott knew the priorities. “The most important thing is safety,” he said. “From the start, I knew the products were really well designed and tested. I mean, this is a German company. They are very rigorous, to say the least, about safety tests.”
The sleek new line appeals to fashion-conscious young mothers like Virginia Galateri di Genola, a trend editor for Italian Vogue’s website and a guest at the event. “They are super-fashion but not too much,” she said. “Super-cool black products with a little touch of gold.”
She continued with a laugh, “My children are too old for the carrier, but my friend and I were thinking maybe we should have a new baby to have these things.”
While Cybex strollers and car seats can be spotted in Milan, Paris and other European fashion capitals, they remain rare in the United States. The car seat wasn’t sold in the United States until 2009, and Mr. Scott’s first collection was sold at
VFiles
, a boutique in SoHo that carries cult streetwear labels.
Back at 10 Corso Como, friends and fans closed in around Mr. Scott, and the D.J. segued to loud hip-hop. A few guests starting dancing, none of whom looked as if they had babies at home.
